title: Sri Chaitanya Upanishad
html:
With the commentary of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura, “Śrī Caitanya-caraṇāmṛta,” and the Bengali translation “Amṛta-bindu”

Translated from Sanskrit and Bengali into English

Sanskrit text, transliteration, word-for-word, translation, and commentary

✦

Translator’s Preface

What this text is. The Śrī Chaitanya Upanishad (in the edition, “Śrī-Śrī-Caitanyopaniṣat”) is a short Upanishad assigned to the Atharva Veda: nineteen brief sections, in prose and verse. Following the pattern of the ancient Upanishads, it is cast as a dialogue: the sage Pippalāda, known as the teacher of the Praśna Upaniṣad, comes to Brahmā asking about the highest good, and then about how the people of the Kali age will be liberated; he is told that in Navadvīpa, on the bank of the Ganges, Govinda Himself will appear as the golden Gaura, in the form of a devotee, to manifest bhakti to the world; that He Himself will repeat the mahā-mantra of sixteen names — “Hare Kṛṣṇa Hare Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Kṛṣṇa Hare Hare, Hare Rāma Hare Rāma Rāma Rāma Hare Hare” — and that whoever serves Him and meditates on Him crosses over māyā. The Upanishad explains the names Hari, Kṛṣṇa, and Rāma, speaks of the Lord’s two potencies, hlādinī and saṁvit, and closes with the teaching of kṣara (the perishable world), akṣara (the living being), and Puruṣottama, who is higher than both and is called Chaitanya. For Gaudiya Vaishnavas it is a Vedic prophecy of the appearance of Śrī Chaitanya.

How Bhaktivinoda found and published it. According to tradition, Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura long sought a manuscript of this rare Upanishad. In 1886 an old copy was sent to him from Sambalpur (Orissa) by Paṇḍita Madhusūdana Dāsa. Bhaktivinoda wrote on it a Sanskrit commentary, “Śrī Caitanya-caraṇāmṛta” (“The Nectar of Śrī Chaitanya’s Feet”), and in 1887 — the four-hundredth anniversary of Mahāprabhu’s appearance (the colophon of the commentary says “in the fourth century of the Chaitanya era”) — printed the Upanishad at his own press, the Śrī Chaitanya Press, at his house “Bhakti Bhavan” in Calcutta, together with the commentary and a Bengali prose translation by Madhusūdana Dāsa himself, entitled “Amṛta-bindu” (“A Drop of Nectar”). As was his custom, Bhaktivinoda signed the commentary with his worldly name, “Kedāra” (Kedarnath Datta).

Contents of this book. Everything the edition contains is translated here: the mūla (the text of the Upanishad); Bhaktivinoda’s commentary in full (its maṅgalācaraṇa, introduction, glosses on all nineteen verses, and colophon); and the Bengali translation “Amṛta-bindu” (with its colophon). Each verse is given in Devanagari, in transliteration, with word-for-word meanings and a translation, followed by the commentary and the “Amṛta-bindu.”

Sources. The 1887 edition could not be found in open access. The translation follows its reprint by Sri Gopinath Gaudiya Math (Mayapur, ed. Sridas Baba, Gaurabda 448, i.e., c. 1934), where the Sanskrit is printed in Bengali script; it reproduces the same contents as the first edition. The text of the Upanishad has been collated with the electronic text of sanskritdocuments.org; variants are noted in the footnotes. Modern translations are neither reproduced nor paraphrased.

On the antiquity of the text. The Upanishad is not in the canonical list of one hundred and eight Upanishads of the Muktikā and was unknown in print before Bhaktivinoda’s edition; therefore many academic scholars regard it as a late composition of the Vaishnava tradition, pointing to its language and ideas (Navadvīpa, hlādinī and saṁvit, the explanations of the names of the mahā-mantra), which are close to the theology of the sixteenth-century Gaudiya Vaishnavas. Those who uphold its authenticity point to old manuscripts — copies found in Varanasi, in particular, are reported. Vedic tradition knows many “minor” Upanishads that became known late. The Gaudiya Vaishnava tradition, following Bhaktivinoda and Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, accepts the Chaitanya Upanishad as śruti bearing witness to Śrī Chaitanya.

Principles of translation. The translation is as literal as possible; words added for coherence are in square brackets. The compressed style of the commentary, built as glosses (a word of the mūla — its explanation), is preserved. Theological explanations follow Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati: Śrī Chaitanya is Kṛṣṇa Himself in the form of a devotee; His form is not material sattva but pure spirit (viśuddha-sattva); the words “Chaitanya is Rudra, Indra…” (v. 15) are not a monistic identification but a statement that He is the source and Lord of all. Sanskrit is transliterated in IAST.
